idiom_name: immutable record nodes + `with` copy constructor + hand-written Path records
implementation_notes: C# supplies the copy mechanics but not the location: a record (or readonly record struct) brings init-only properties, value equality and a compiler-generated copy constructor, so rebuilding the parent is `b with { Kids = b.Kids.SetItem(i, focus) }` with System.Collections.Immutable providing child lists that share their unchanged structure, and a switch expression over the record shapes drives navigation. What replaces the classic structure is therefore only the copy-and-rebuild half; the context - a stack of frames recording the parent record and the child index - is still hand-written, and the classic mutable-node form (WPF/WinForms object graphs updated in place) stays justified when a single thread owns the tree and copying it would be pure overhead.
pitfalls: Record equality and GetHashCode are structural and recursive: comparing two locations, or using them as dictionary keys, walks the whole tree and can overflow the stack on deep trees.
`with` copies member references, not contents - a record holding List<T> still shares that mutable list with the copy; only ImmutableList or a hand-written copy constructor prevents it.
Nullable reference types and the ^1 indexer hide that Path[^1] on an empty path throws at runtime, so "at the root" is a checked case, not an exception to discover in production.
A large node as a record struct is copied on every assignment and cannot use a compiler-synthesized copy constructor, so record struct pays off only for small value-like nodes.
